rows.en: Simeon the Just is praised with many praises. He was a man who walked whole-heartedly with God, and in love and kindness with men (Josephus, ibid.). And as he himself cleaved to the Torah of the Lord, served his God with a whole heart and did kindness to men, so he taught his people and instructed them to walk in this way to which his foot held fast. The preciousness of these foundations and the greatness of their worth he described in a short saying, after the manner of the ancients, when he said: "On three things the world stands: on the Torah, on the service, and on deeds of lovingkindness" (Avot ch. 1). This saying, by its inner content, bears the stamp of the longing of his spirit and of the needs of his time; and by its form one already finds in it the pattern of the sayings ascribed to the Scribes, in that they are counted out item by item. He very strongly condemned outward service in the performance of the commandments, and praised those who perform them if they do them with attention and with a pure mind. For this very reason he took no pleasure in those who vowed naziriteship to mortify themselves. Therefore all his days he refrained from eating the offering of a nazirite, for he said that whoever lays a prohibition on himself by naziriteship is counted a sinner. He was the man who laid the cornerstone of the rule that those who came after him stated at a later time, that whoever sits in a fast is called a sinner (Nedarim 10a). Once a man came to him from the South, with beautiful eyes and of good appearance, his locks curled, and he was a nazirite. Simeon the Just said to him: "What did you see, my son, to destroy this beautiful hair?" He told him: "I was a shepherd in my town, and I went to draw water from the spring, and I saw my reflection in the water, and my inclination rose wantonly against me and sought to drive me out of the world. I said to it: Wicked one, you are swelling with pride over something that is not yours! It is upon me to consecrate you to Heaven." Simeon bowed his head to him and said to him: "My son, may those who do the will of the Place multiply in Israel like you! Of you the verse says: 'a nazirite, to separate himself to the Lord' [Numbers 6:2]" (Nedarim and Nazir ch. 1, Bavli and Yerushalmi, and Sifre Naso, and in many places). We see from this with how much insight Simeon went deeply into the words of the Torah. For when the Torah said "a nazirite, to separate himself to the Lord," it does not mean that if a man mortifies himself for the honor of Heaven the Lord has pleasure in it; rather, the meaning is that the naziriteship by which a man separates himself is truly "to the Lord" when the one who vows the naziriteship has a moral reason for it. The form of this aggadah bears on its face the stamp of its antiquity, and perhaps the words that the narrator put in Simeon's mouth were his very words; then it would appear from this that already in his days they were accustomed to use the word "Heaven" to name God who dwells in heaven, and likewise the name "Place" for the name of the Lord. There is no doubt that these two names are not native to the Hebrews. In particular the name "Heaven" for the name of the Lord is a metaphor taken from the Greeks, who call heaven and the God of heaven by one name. And their fear of pronouncing the Name in its letters was the reason why they sought for themselves various names by which to call the Name.

From the effort that Simeon made to hold the people back from naziriteship we may rightly judge that at that time they were very unrestrained in vows and naziriteships, as we shall see in the generations after him, in the days of the war of the Maccabees, when there were people who had vowed naziriteship and came to Jerusalem to complete the days of their naziriteship (1 Maccabees 3:49). This licence, in which a man loads mortifications on himself by vows and naziriteship, is for the most part a sign of the hardships of the time and of the troubles breaking out. For from of old men thought that by laying a prohibition on themselves and afflicting themselves with mortifications and self-denial they would obtain favor from God, that He would have mercy on them and save them from their troubles. This thought took root in them because they saw that all religions and faiths in general, and the divine religion in particular, lay prohibitions on a man's soul and command statutes whose performance depends on things from which they impose restraint. And because they saw that, according to the promise of the giver of the religion, keeping these statutes and restraint from forbidden things are the fitting ways to obtain God's grace and favor, they thought that the more they forbade themselves even things permitted to them by religion, the more they would find grace in God's eyes and obtain His favor, so that for this He would be a help to them in trouble. Therefore, as the hardships multiplied from then on, so those who vowed vows and naziriteships multiplied. Now we have seen that Simeon the Just had no liking for these, and opposed those who vowed naziriteships and vows, who were rife in his days. So it is not wondrous nor far-fetched if we suppose that in that time they enacted that the sage would have authority to release vows. For when they saw that the people were unrestrained in vows, they enacted that the sage has power to release the vow upon the regret of the one who vowed, saying that it was an error. And although the release of vows has no clear and explicit proof from the Torah, there is surely a hint of the matter: the Torah gave power to the father to annul his daughter's vows and to the husband to annul his wife's vows; therefore they decided by reasoning that likewise the sage would have power to release the vows of the people, who are led by the sages of the generations. By force of this reasoning they enacted the ordinance of the release of vows. The early masters of the Mishnah already knew that this ordinance was new, only the forgetting that came in the wake of the hardships caused the time of the enactment to be hidden from them; therefore they said (Ḥagigah, end of ch. 1): "The release of vows floats in the air and has nothing to rest on." But it seems that there were among the sages of the generations some who, although they strove to hold back vows, did not think it right to agree that one who vowed a vow should go to the sage to release it. One of the sages who spoke against the bad custom of those who vow vows was the author of the book of Ecclesiastes. We already know that this book was composed at the end of the days of the Persian kings (above, ch. 1, in the note), and he says explicitly that a man ought to guard the door of his lips from vowing a vow. Of vows of consecration and the like he says: "Better is it that you should not vow, than that you should vow and not pay" (Ecclesiastes 5:4). But of the vows that men vow to lay a prohibition on themselves and to mortify themselves, of these he warns that one should not vow at all, and that a man should not "suffer his mouth to cause his flesh to sin" [Ecclesiastes 5:5], to mortify and afflict himself,{v1_05_15:1} and should not be forced to annul the words of his mouth and to go before "the messenger" [Ecclesiastes 5:5], that is, the sage who teaches, who bears this name also in the later prophets (Haggai 1:13; Malachi 2:6⚠1), and to say that what he vowed was an error, because he vowed in his haste and now regrets it and wants the sage to annul his vow. We see from this that when the book of Ecclesiastes was composed, the ordinance of the release of vows was not yet a settled and accepted ordinance; therefore our supposition is very likely, that in the days of Simeon the Just they made it a fixed ordinance, because they saw that the hour required it.

1.note: The priest called 'messenger of the Lord' is Malachi 2:7; reference kept as printed.

rows.en: One of the exalted virtues for which those who told his history praised him is the virtue of prophecy, for they said of him that the holy spirit spoke in him. In the last year of his priesthood,{v1_05_16:1} when he came out of the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement, he prophesied that he would die in that year. And so it was: seven days after the festival of Sukkot the righteous man went to his eternal home and was buried at a good old age. They mourned very greatly over his death, for he left no righteous man among the living who equaled him; the priests lamented that a loss had been lost that could not be replaced. For this very reason his brothers the priests refrained from then on from blessing with the Explicit Name (Yoma 39b, and Yerushalmi there, ch. 6). It has not become clear to us what the particular reason for this refraining was, but this much comes out explicitly from the content of the story: because they saw that faith and the fear of Heaven had diminished, they thought that neither they nor their generation were worthy to pronounce the Name explicitly, even in the Priestly Blessing, and they refrained from pronouncing it although they had been specially commanded about it. For to pronounce the Name in its letters as it is written — for the rest of the people, or also for the priests outside the Priestly Blessing — they already refrained in the time of the first Scribes, and this too was among their ordinances. Just as they ordained various substitute names in order to give honor to the name of the Lord, sometimes by a change in the reading and sometimes also in writing, so they ordained a substitute for the Explicit Name of the Lord, so that it should not be read as it is written. But in the blessing with which the priests were commanded to bless Israel, they pronounced the Name; and already at that time they understood the Torah's words "Thus shall you bless the children of Israel" [Numbers 6:23] to mean: "thus," with precision, the words as they are written, and therefore they must bless with the Name as it is written (Sifre, portion Naso, piska 25⚠1). And it is said explicitly: "And they shall put My name upon the children of Israel" [Numbers 6:27] (Sotah 38a). It is clear that these verses were already expounded in this way by the ancient Scribes, since we see that until the death of Simeon the Just they blessed with the Explicit Name, although already from then on they refrained from pronouncing the Name as it is written. Yet although they understood the verse to mean that it is a commandment to bless with the Explicit Name, and did so until the death of Simeon, nevertheless they abolished this commandment and refrained from blessing with the Name. It is true that the later sages (Sotah 38a, Tosafot s.v. harei) try to show that this was not an uprooting or abolition of the commandment by an ordinance of the sages, but that they abolished it relying on the will of the Torah itself. For according to their view, and according to what they derived by the ways of midrash elsewhere, they decided that the name of the Lord may not be mentioned in any case except in a place and at a time where there is a revelation of the Shekhinah; and since, in the priests' view, the revelation of the Shekhinah ceased after the death of Simeon the Just,{v1_05_16:2} this commandment was abolished by the law of the Torah itself. But if we consider the words of the Talmudic sages themselves, we find that they did not think, and it did not occur to them to say, that from the days of Simeon the revelation of the Shekhinah ceased in the Temple. We have no proof or hint that any of the masters of the Talmud thought or believed so, and all the more we have no hint that the priests after Simeon's death thought that with his death the Shekhinah departed from the Temple. But in truth it is as we said: the particular reason that the priests had for not pronouncing the Name when they blessed the people has not been preserved for us; but this lies in the nature of the matter, that as they raised Simeon's standing after his death, so, over against his standing, they made their own standing small, and thought that neither they nor their generation were worthy to pronounce the Name even in the Priestly Blessing.

1.note: The exegesis of 'thus' (koh) stands in Sifre Numbers §39 in the usual editions; kept as printed.

rows.en: From the few things that have been told us of the standing of Simeon the Just, and from the aggadot attached to his name, it has become clear that he was the most distinguished of all the heads of the generations in the days of the Great Assembly. Therefore without doubt his time too was distinguished by excellent ordinances enacted for the good of the nation, and it is very likely that the ordinance of the closing of the Holy Scriptures was also the work of his time. For from the time that they went up from the exile, led by Ezra the Scribe, the Torah struck its roots in the heart of every man of Israel, and these roots spread over the land of Israel; and then everyone called by the name of Israel was stirred to hold fast to the teachings of the men of understanding. And although there were among them adversaries who harassed them with their wiles, namely the Kutim [Samaritans], whom the king of Assyria settled in the cities of Samaria and who accepted and took upon themselves the religion of Israel, these too lacked strength, and it was not in their power to do anything, great or small, to disturb Israel in their faith. "From the time of Nehemiah until the days of the reign of Alexander they did not then separate in complete separation from the Jews, and some of them celebrated their festivals in Jerusalem" (Kirchheim, in *Karmei Shomron*, p. 2). And there were no other challengers among them against the customs and views of the Jews who would force them to publish some ordinance meant to show opposition to some challenge. "From the days of Alexander of Macedon they — these Kutim — began to call themselves by their own names over the land, and became a lowly kingdom to do evil to Israel — and their temple on Mount Gerizim was a snare and a trap to the inhabitant of Jerusalem. And without doubt at that time was made the copy of the book of the Torah that is in their hands, with the variants and changes without which there would be no basis or root for their worship and their sanctuary" (*Karmei Shomron*, pp. 2–7). And perhaps they made the falsifications already before the time of Alexander, for when Alexander came to Syria their temple already stood on Mount Gerizim, and without the falsifications they made there is no place for worship on Mount Gerizim. Besides the variants and changes that they falsified in the Torah, they opposed the Jews in another matter, which is a great foundation among the principles of the Jewish religion: they denied the prophecy of the other prophets and did not accept their books. Now the falsifications they made in the Torah, and likewise their opposition to the books of the Prophets, were a great cause that moved the sages of the generation to make a fence and a safeguard in this, and to hold with all the strength of their might to the true text of the Torah — and who knows whether the Men of the Great Assembly did not mean this in their saying "Make a fence for the Torah," to warn against falsification, variation and change — and further, to proclaim widely the error of the Kutim and of those Jews who followed them in denying the holiness of the rest of the Holy Scriptures and the books of the Prophets; and they were forced to make known and to declare publicly that all of them are holy and were hewn from a divine source. Now this was one of the causes that compelled them to gather together the number of the Holy Scriptures and to join them together in the holy collection. And the closing [seal] of the Holy Scriptures alludes to this, namely the last four verses of the book of Ecclesiastes (*Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, gate 11), where it says: "The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails well fastened are the masters of assemblies; they are given from one shepherd" [Ecclesiastes 12:11]. This is a great hint of their intention, to say: that all the words in the Writings flowed from one spirit and their foundation is in holiness. But they had yet another reason to close the Holy Scriptures: from the time the Greeks came to the land of Judah, new views were brought to them, some of which found favor in the eyes of the Jews and their sages, and some of which were dangerous to the Torah and to the faith. Their acquaintance with these views no doubt stirred the hearts of the seekers of wisdom and of the writers among the Jews to follow them in their inquiries, and they also wrote books or essays on the foundations of foreign views such as these. Therefore they were compelled to set a fence and a hedge around the Torah and the authenticated Holy Scriptures, and to guard their unity with extra care, out of worry lest holy seed mingle with profane seed, and books written according to new views be joined to the holy books whose issue is from the spirit of God. And they made it a statute not to be transgressed, that to the accepted Holy Scriptures nothing may be added and from them nothing may be taken away. Now for this reason the second verse of the aforementioned closing also gives a hint, warning: "And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end" [Ecclesiastes 12:12]. Its meaning is to warn against making books beyond our holy books, for only they have their foundation in holiness, and apart from them they are "much study, a weariness of the flesh" [ibid.]. Now the closing of the Holy Scriptures is not to be put later than the time of the end of the Great Assembly, and that is about fifty years after the Greeks settled in Syria and in the Land. True, it would have been proper for them to bring order to the matter already in the earlier time, since occupation with the Torah was a fixed statute and counted a great commandment, and they also ordained the reading in the Torah and in the Prophets and made translations for the common people; therefore it would have been self-evident that it was fitting to clarify, to arrange and to make known which books were designated for fulfilling the commandment and to be read by religious law.{v1_05_18:1} But the truth is that in early times there was no need for the closing, because they had no reason to worry lest the profane mix with the holy; but in the time we are dealing with the matter was reversed, therefore they were forced to bring order to the matter and to set a fixed statute which books are holy and divine.

footnotes.en: See Mekhilta, Mishpatim ch. 4, which expounded "you shall take him from My altar, that he may die" [Exodus 21:14]: to die, and not to be tried⚠1. And in Berakhot (32b) they expounded "your hands are full of blood" [Isaiah 1:15]: a priest who killed a person is unfit to lift up his hands [in the Priestly Blessing], and all the more he is unfit for the Temple service; see Sanhedrin (35a) and Tosafot. In any case, and according to all views, it is plain that a priest who killed a person is not to be allowed to the service in the first place, and all the more, if he is a high priest, that he must be removed. And all these halakhot and laws cannot be reconciled with the story told in the text.

1.note: Literal; the sense seems to be that he is taken from the altar for execution, not merely for trial.

footnotes.en: Concerning their stand against the Kutim [Samaritans] we shall speak below, how this sect was a cause of new ordinances and statutes among the Jews.

See what Zunz wrote, G. V.⚠1, p. 36; Herzfeld's history of the Jews [*Geschichte des Volkes Israel*], vol. 2, p. 195; and Jost's history of the Jewish religion and the sects [*Geschichte des Judenthums und seiner Secten*], vol. 1, p. 95. And in the journal *Ben Chananja*, first year, p. 198, R. Leibush Löw supposes that the Simeon who was of the remnants of the Great Assembly is Simeon the Hasmonean.

1.note: Abbreviation printed thus; most likely Zunz, Gottesdienstliche Vorträge.

footnotes.en: The meaning of the phrase "to cause your flesh to sin" is not from the sense of sin, that is, that a man should not give his mouth to bring himself into sin by the speech of his mouth; rather it seems more likely that the root ḥeṭ here has the sense of destruction, as in "he who provokes him to anger sins against his own soul" (Proverbs 20:2), where the meaning is that one who provokes the king destroys his own soul; and likewise "and you have sinned against your soul" (Habakkuk 2:10).

According to the Talmud, Simeon the Just served in the high priesthood forty years; but Zunz and other scholars of antiquity have proved that he did not serve in the high priesthood more than twenty years. And I have seen fit to point out here what we wrote in *Ha-Tsofeh le-Ha-Maggid* of the year [5]627, no. 32, p. 253: that all the aggadot that tell about Simeon the Just in Yoma (39a), in Tosefta Sotah ch. 3 and in Yerushalmi Yoma 6:3, concerning the changes that came after his death in the matter of the lot on the Day of Atonement, the western lamp, the fire of the altar pile, the Omer, the Two Loaves and the Showbread — all this refers neither to the first Simeon the Just nor to the second, but to another Simeon the Just who lived at a later time, in the days of the Roman emperor Caligula, about thirty years before the destruction of the Temple. And see Megillat Ta'anit ch. 11.

In Tosafot there they relied on the midrash on "In every place where I cause My name to be mentioned" etc. [Exodus 20:21], where they transpose the verse: in every place where I am revealed, I command that My name be mentioned. Therefore after the death of Simeon the Just, when there was no longer a revelation of the Shekhinah and they no longer merited the revelation of the Shekhinah, they refrained from blessing with the Name. There is no doubt that the Tosafot have in mind the aggadot that tell of a number of miracles that ceased after the death of Simeon the Just; but we have already shown in the previous note that all this does not refer to the first Simeon the Just. According to the view of the Tosafot they no longer merited the revelation of the Shekhinah after Simeon's death even in the Temple, and it was not included in "every place where I cause My name to be mentioned"; but this is contradicted by the baraita in Sukkah (53a) and by the Mekhilta, Yitro ch. 11 — see there in our work *Middot Soferim* — and we have not found any of the Talmudic sages who says that there was some time when the Holy One, blessed be He, was not revealed in the chosen house. The main point is that the view of the authors of the baraita here is that "in every place where I cause My name to be mentioned" etc. does not mean to exclude any time, for according to the Talmud there was no time in all the days of the Temple when the Holy One, blessed be He, did not cause His Shekhinah to dwell in it; it means only to exclude the place, that is, that outside the Temple it is forbidden to do so.
